desc:
A grid of letters is given as an integer matrix board (1 is a, 2 is b, ..., 26 is z).

A path that spells word uses one cell per letter, in order. Every cell after the first must be directly above, below, left or right of the previous cell, and a cell may not be used twice in the same path. Return the number of different paths that spell word; paths are different when they use different cells or the same cells in a different order.

For example, in the board [[1,1],[1,1]] the word aaa can be spelled in 8 ways (4 starting cells, and from each one the path can turn clockwise or counterclockwise), and in [[1,2],[2,1]] the word ab can be spelled in 4 ways.
hints: Decide a start cell, then every later letter has at most 3 possible next cells. Counting paths is the same search as finding one, except that you keep going after you succeed.

Write go(r, c, k): the number of ways to spell word[k:] when the path stands on cell (r, c) and that cell already matches word[k]. At k == L - 1 return 1; otherwise mark the cell, add up go over the unvisited neighbours that match word[k + 1], and unmark the cell.
Never recurse into a neighbour whose letter does not match: this prunes almost the whole tree for ordinary words. Sum go over every start cell whose letter is word[0].
editorial: The classic word search asks whether a path exists and may stop at the first one. Counting asks for all of them, so the search must not stop early: every branch that matches the next letter is explored, and the results are added. A DFS with a visited grid does this, and un-marking the cell on the way back lets other paths reuse it (that is the backtracking part).

A memo table keyed on (cell, k) would be wrong here, because the number of ways to finish depends on which cells have already been used, not only on the current cell and position. Instead the running time is proportional to the number of partial paths that match a prefix of the word, at most m * n * 3L-1, and the small limits (5 x 5 board, word length at most 9) keep that fast.
